title: IB English Individual Oral Prep Timeline for Fall
summary: Use this IB English Individual Oral prep timeline to plan global issues, extracts, analysis, outlines, and rehearsals from September to November.
body_markdown:
If your IB English Individual Oral takes place in November, begin focused preparation in **early September** . This gives you approximately **8-10 weeks** to choose a defensible global issue, test extracts, develop analysis, and rehearse alongside your other IB subjects.


An effective **IB English Individual Oral prep timeline** does not begin with writing a script. It begins with reviewing eligible texts and identifying connections that support detailed analysis. The schedule below assumes a late-November oral, but your teacher's deadlines always take priority.


### Know the Individual Oral requirements


The Individual Oral is a **15-minute internal assessment** . You deliver a prepared response for **10 minutes** , followed by approximately **5 minutes of teacher questions** . Your teacher assesses it, and the IB externally moderates the marking.


The oral is worth **30% at SL** and **20% at HL** in English A: Language and Literature and English A: Literature. Four criteria assess knowledge and interpretation, analysis and evaluation, focus and organization, and language. Each criterion is worth 10 marks, producing **40 marks** overall.


Course Required pairing


English A: Language and Literature One literary work and one non-literary body of work


English A: Literature One work originally written in the language studied and one work studied in translation


Both texts must connect through a common **global issue** . You use one extract from each to analyze how authorial choices construct meaning, while also connecting each extract to the wider work or body of work.


The[official Language and Literature subject brief](https://www.ibo.org/contentassets/5895a05412144fe890312bad52b17044/curriculum.brief-languagea.language.and.literature-eng.pdf) and[official Literature subject brief](https://www.ibo.org/contentassets/5895a05412144fe890312bad52b17044/curriculum.brief-languagea.literature-eng.pdf) confirm the pairings and weightings. Ask your teacher about eligible works, recording dates, extract formatting, and submission procedures.


### September-to-November IB English Individual Oral prep timeline


### Early September: review texts and global issues


During the first two weeks, review completed works and bodies of work before committing to a pairing. Note recurring conflicts, perspectives, and authorial choices.


Test each possibility by asking:


- Is the issue significant beyond the immediate characters or setting?
- Does it have transnational significance and local consequences?
- Can I analyze several authorial choices in both texts?
- Can each extract connect to meaningful patterns elsewhere?


A field such as **politics, power and justice** is not a sufficiently precise global issue. “Power” is also too broad. A stronger formulation is “the normalization of surveillance as a means of suppressing political dissent,” provided that both texts clearly explore it.


Use the fields of inquiry as starting points. RevisionDojo's[guide to IB English fields of inquiry](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/understanding-the-fields-of-inquiry-in-ib-english-a-guide-for-the-individual-oral) explains how to refine a broad category into a focused issue.


**Target by mid-September:** two possible pairings with one or two global issues for each.


### Late September: test and select extracts


Locate several possible extracts from each text. A strong extract does more than contain a relevant event. It concentrates analyzable choices in language, form, structure, imagery, voice, framing, typography, sound, or editing.


For written works, extracts should normally not exceed **40 lines** . Confirm the required presentation of poems, photographs, advertisements, and multimodal texts with your teacher.


Score each candidate against four questions:


1. Is the global issue clearly present?
2. Can I discuss **3-5 significant authorial choices** ?
3. Does it connect naturally to the wider work?
4. Can I analyze it without rushing?


Give each serious candidate a 90-second spoken test. If you can only summarize events, reconsider it. If you can explain how choices shape the audience's understanding, it is more promising.


**Target by late September:** an approved issue, pairing, and two extracts.


### Early October: develop close and wider analysis


Organize analysis around a consistent reasoning chain:


**authorial choice → evidence → effect → interpretation → global issue**


Naming fragmented syntax, for example, is insufficient. Explain how it represents disrupted thought, affects the audience, and develops the global issue. Depth comes from explaining relationships rather than listing techniques.


Prepare **2-3 central claims** for each extract. Then identify wider moments that establish recurrence, contrast, development, or complication. The[IB discussion of intertextuality and intratextuality](https://blogs.ibo.org/2019/07/12/intertextuality-and-intratextuality-ii-the-individual-oral/) clarifies why extracts should support understanding of the wider works rather than remain isolated passages.


**Target by mid-October:** a thesis, detailed annotations, and at least two purposeful wider-work connections per text.


### Late October: construct the 10-minute argument


Reduce your research into a balanced structure:


Section Suggested time Purpose


Introduction 1 minute Define the issue, texts, and central argument


First text 4 minutes Analyze the extract and wider work


Second text 4 minutes Analyze the extract and wider work or body of work


Conclusion 1 minute Synthesize the texts' treatment of the issue


This division is practical advice, not an IB-mandated formula. It prevents an overlong introduction and protects balance.


Prepare the official outline according to your teacher's instructions, observing the limit of **no more than 10 bullet points** . Use concise prompts containing claims, brief evidence, and analytical links. Do not disguise a script as extended bullets.


The[RevisionDojo step-by-step IO guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-approach-the-ib-english-individual-oral-io-presentation-a-step-by-step-guide) offers further help with structuring evidence.


**Target by late October:** a complete outline and first timed recording.


### Early November: revise using the criteria


Review your recording one criterion at a time:


- Check that interpretations and contextual references are accurate.
- Replace device spotting with explanations of constructed meaning.
- Remove repetition and rebalance the two texts.
- Use precise analytical language while sounding natural.


Do not memorize a polished script word for word. Learn the sequence of claims and the purpose of each bullet instead. RevisionDojo's[guide to IO assessment](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/understanding-the-assessment-of-your-ib-individual-oral-io) can help you diagnose weaknesses by criterion.


**Target by mid-November:** two complete recordings followed by targeted revisions.


### Final 7-10 days: rehearse delivery and questions


Stop adding major arguments unless you find a genuine gap. Complete a structure run, an analysis run, and a full simulation consisting of 10 minutes speaking plus 5 minutes of questions.


Questions may ask you to clarify an interpretation, justify a technique's significance, or connect another part of a work to the issue. Prepare through understanding rather than memorized answers. The[RevisionDojo IO practice tool guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-io-practice-tool-perfect-your-individual-oral-skills-with-ai) explains a record, review, and repeat process, while Jojo AI can generate follow-up questions.


### Common preparation mistakes


Avoid choosing a theme instead of a precise global issue, selecting extracts for dramatic plot events, summarizing instead of analyzing, or ignoring the wider work. Other frequent problems include unbalanced coverage, excessive historical context, script memorization, and silent practice without a timer.


If you are starting only three weeks before the oral, finalize the issue and extracts within three days. Use the next week for analysis, the second for outlining and recording, and the final week for criterion-based revision and question practice.


### Conclusion


For a November oral, start in **early September** , finalize extracts by late September, and use October for close analysis and wider-work connections. Reserve November for timed delivery and questions. RevisionDojo's[comprehensive IB Oral guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/comprehensive-guide-to-the-ib-individual-oral-io-for-language-and-literature-and-literature) , Jojo AI, and the IO practice workflow can support planning and rehearsal once your own interpretation is established.
